summary: Keep every project file on a server under a management tool that locks, merges and backs up edits, and still expect lost changes, because big teams collide on shared files all the time.
takeaways: Large games span up to millions of files and hundreds of people
Lock a file while editing, upload and unlock when done
Auto-merge conflicting edits, then fix leftover discrepancies by hand
Reverted changes are common; recover them from version backups

principles.principle: Track all game files on a server with lock-edit-upload-unlock
principles.why: A large game has tens of thousands to millions of files and can have hundreds of people editing them, so you need a tool that stops two people from editing the same file at once.
principles.how: Put every file under a management tool: editing a file locks it, and uploading the finished edit back to the server unlocks it.
principles.anti_pattern: Sharing files by hand with no locking or tracking.
principles.quote: When someone's editing a file, that file gets locked.

principles.principle: Merge simultaneous edits to big files and resolve leftovers manually
principles.why: Letting only one person work on a particularly large file is inefficient, and conflicting uploads happen anyway.
principles.how: Allow concurrent edits on large files, let the tool compare and stitch the edits together, and have someone fix any discrepancies the merge can't resolve.
principles.anti_pattern: Keeping a huge shared file locked to one person while others wait.

principles.principle: Expect edits to get reverted and recover them from version history
principles.why: Reversion, where changes vanish and the file returns to its pre-edit state, is a common occurrence even though the tools should work in theory.
principles.how: When a change goes missing, go back a version: the tool backs up every edit, so the lost work can often be retrieved.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming the management tool makes lost changes impossible.
principles.quote: There shouldn't be any issues, in theory— but in practice, it's a constant source of headaches.

summary: Teach your controls by letting players play the real game while they learn, not through manual-style text or a separate training room, and protect that hands-on tutorial in the schedule.
takeaways: A tutorial is essential, but nobody wants hand-holding
Long manual-style text is the worst way to teach
Separate training rooms make players beg for the real game
Let players play the game while you teach them
Sakurai's biggest regret: Ultimate's cut hands-on tutorial

principles.principle: Teach controls inside real gameplay, never in a manual-style text wall
principles.why: Players don't want to sit through hand-holding or read long paragraphs, and an inorganic training area just makes them want the real game.
principles.how: Place short prompts along the path of the opening stage so players read them and immediately put them into practice; use richer hands-on methods for complex controls.
principles.anti_pattern: Long instruction-manual paragraphs or a detached practice room.
principles.example: Smash Bros. uses only a non-interactive video, which Sakurai considers a compromise.
principles.quote: At any rate, I'd say it's vital that you let players play the game as you teach them.

principles.principle: Build modes that double as hands-on control training
principles.why: A playable challenge teaches the controls through doing, rather than telling.
principles.how: Design a challenge around each character's specific moves so clearing it requires using them, as Break the Targets! did.
principles.example: Break the Targets! in the first Super Smash Bros. was designed to help players master the controls, so it's different for each character.

principles.principle: Schedule the hands-on tutorial as a must-ship feature
principles.why: Hands-on tutorials for Smash were planned many times and cut, and losing the Ultimate technique mode to the schedule is a lasting regret.
principles.how: Lock the playable tutorial into the schedule early instead of treating it as an extra that can be dropped near the end.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving tutorial work until late, when schedule pressure cuts it.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's planned hands-on technique mode was dropped for schedule reasons.
principles.quote: I still regret that, even now.

summary: Shallow depth of field and high saturation make things look small, so to make large objects feel big, keep blur out of the frame, lower the saturation of big and distant objects, and judge scale on the whole final image.
takeaways: Blur, high saturation and less blue make things look miniature
Avoid shallow depth of field except in specific spots
Lower saturation on large, distant objects for aerial perspective
Judge scale on the whole final image, not textures

principles.principle: Lower saturation on large, distant objects to sell their scale
principles.why: Large objects have aerial perspective, so full saturation makes them look small; the closer an object, the higher its saturation should be.
principles.how: Reduce saturation and let bluish haze build with distance on big objects and vistas, and keep the most vivid colors near the camera.
principles.anti_pattern: Giving huge distant objects the same vivid saturation as nearby ones.
principles.example: Miniature photo demo: raising saturation and cutting blue hues makes a landscape look like a model.
principles.quote: To put it another way, the closer an object is to you, the higher its saturation should be.

principles.principle: Avoid shallow depth of field except where truly needed
principles.why: People focus on different parts of a composition, and trying to focus on something blurry can be physically uncomfortable; blur also makes scenes look miniature.
principles.how: Remove depth-of-field blur and focus pulls from gameplay and trailer shots unless one specific location requires it.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding depth of field everywhere as an atmosphere boost.
principles.example: In Sora's fighter reveal, a focus shift from background to foreground was removed at Sakurai's request.

principles.principle: Check scale on the final composed image, not per texture
principles.why: Drawing each material's texture on its own won't produce cohesive visuals, and scale is something Sakurai has to correct often.
principles.how: Review scenes as full frames or screenshots and adjust saturation and blur across the whole image.
principles.anti_pattern: Polishing individual textures without stepping back.

summary: Use the genre's de facto standard controls so you can skip explaining what players already know, but still support newcomers and let everyone remap buttons.
takeaways: Standard controls let you skip explanations players don't need
Use industry de facto standards instead of avoiding copying
Remember some players are new to your genre
Always offer button remapping, even if it's complicated
Analog-dependent games can't simply move to a D-pad

principles.principle: Adopt your genre's de facto standard controls
principles.why: Players who already know the conventions need no explanation, which warms up the handshake between human and computer.
principles.how: Map core actions to the buttons the genre has standardized (as FPS games do with fire and grenade) unless you have a deliberate reason not to.
principles.anti_pattern: Inventing a new layout only to avoid copying other games.
principles.example: Western FPS games share nearly the same control scheme.
principles.quote: By doing so, you're making the handshake between human and computer just a little bit warmer.

principles.principle: Skip explanations of conventions players already know
principles.why: Omitting or abridging what players know is a great advantage, though some players will be new to the genre.
principles.how: Drop text like 'your guns need ammo'; at most show the attack-button icon when the first enemy appears, and still check onboarding with genre newcomers.
principles.anti_pattern: Spelling out every basic genre rule.
principles.example: Few FPS games tell you to fire with R2 or throw a grenade with L1.

principles.principle: Always ship button remapping
principles.why: Designers used to think their controls were the best and nobody would change them, but players want the freedom to play how they like.
principles.how: Add a remapping option to the settings even though it makes things more complicated.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming your default layout is perfect for everyone.

summary: Creators, you included, change paths as they gain experience, so don't write off people who leave games as washed up, and give yourself room to try new fields too.
takeaways: Many creators leave games partway through their careers
Those who vanish often succeed in other fields
Don't begrudge creators for not doing what fans want
Starting something new with experience is natural

principles.principle: Don't write off creators who leave the industry
principles.why: Many who disappear go on to succeed elsewhere, securing lucrative patents or making groundbreaking advances in unrelated fields.
principles.how: When a creator drops out of view, assume they may be doing fulfilling work somewhere else rather than calling them finished.
principles.anti_pattern: Labeling vanished creators as washed up or finished.
principles.example: Former colleagues who secured patents or made advances outside games.
principles.quote: please don't write them off as “washed up” or “finished”!

principles.principle: Let yourself start something new as your experience grows
principles.why: Staying put for a whole career is less common than moving on, and everyone has the right to choose their own path.
principles.how: Take on a new kind of project outside your usual field while keeping your main work going, as Sakurai did with his YouTube channel.
principles.anti_pattern: Expecting yourself or other creators to keep doing only what fans want.
principles.example: Sakurai started this YouTube channel while still making games.

summary: Answer every review request the same day it arrives, first come first served, so you never stall your team, and set aside a fixed block of time when you do no reviews at all.
takeaways: Request reviews by email titled 'Review Request'
Handle requests first come, first served
Reply to every review request within the same day
Delayed decisions can put a whole team behind
Reserve a no-review block for your own tasks

principles.principle: Answer every review request within the same day
principles.why: Slow replies keep team members waiting, delaying a key member's decision can put a whole team behind, and fast replies make later review rounds easier.
principles.how: Reply as soon as a request arrives, or right after the review you're on; never let unread requests carry over to the next day.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting review emails accumulate, which also makes the next day more miserable.
principles.example: Sakurai responds to every review email the same day no matter how many pile up.
principles.quote: But no matter how many come in, and no matter how many pile up, I've always made it a point to respond to them within the same day.

principles.principle: Use one fixed channel and first-come order for review requests
principles.why: Instant messaging and ticketing systems each have drawbacks; a single predictable process keeps reviews fair and trackable.
principles.how: Have team members email a 'Review Request' when production work is finished, handle them in arrival order, and explain any changes to everyone involved.
principles.example: Sakurai's email-only Review Request workflow.

principles.principle: Reserve a daily block with no reviews for your own work
principles.why: Review emails arrive in erratic bursts that fragment a director's schedule, and directors have plenty of non-supervision work.
principles.how: Pick a timeframe, such as mornings or after a set cutoff, when you stop reviewing and work only on your own tasks.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving yourself open for supervision all day long.

summary: Use Caillois's four elements of play (competition, chance, imitation and vertigo) as a checklist: build your core around clever competitive play, then add chance, real-world imitation and visceral sensation on top.
takeaways: Play has four elements: agon, alea, mimicry, ilinx
Game essence (push and pull) is mainly agon
Clever plays, not physical advantage, should decide winners
Mimicry enriches information; ilinx makes play feel visceral
Purposeless play is anything but meaningless

principles.principle: Let clever plays, not raw advantage, decide the winner
principles.why: Game essence, or push and pull, is primarily agon (competition), and in Sakurai's view it is clever plays rather than physical advantage that should decide the victor.
principles.how: Tune competitive mechanics so reads, timing and positioning can overcome stat or size advantages.
principles.anti_pattern: Outcomes decided mainly by who has the bigger numbers.
principles.quote: It's not simply physical advantage, but clever plays that decide the victor.

principles.principle: Layer chance, imitation and vertigo onto your competitive core
principles.why: Agon alone isn't all of play; alea, mimicry and ilinx each add a distinct kind of fun that Sakurai's games also rely on.
principles.how: Audit your game for all four elements and add what's missing, such as randomly appearing items that can influence the outcome (alea).
principles.example: Randomly appearing items in Sakurai's games influence the outcome.

principles.principle: Imitate reality so objects and actions carry rich information
principles.why: Mimicry increases the density and richness of a game's information because players read things the way they exist in reality.
principles.how: Make floors look hard, windups look powerful and hits sound painful.

principles.principle: Build visceral payoffs and fear into play
principles.why: Ilinx, or vertigo, is what makes a game feel viscerally good.
principles.how: Create strong knockback moments after a tough struggle and real danger around falling.
principles.example: Knocking an enemy back after a tough struggle; the fear of falling.

summary: Give every swing a blade trail that suits the weapon, built as a fading polygon ribbon (or a one-frame flat image for instant swings), and adjust the animation until the trail reads clearly, because attacks lose their oomph without one.
takeaways: Build trails as polygon fans behind the blade
Fade the trail's tail with translucency
Adjust animations; plain horizontal slashes read poorly
Use a flat 2D mesh for one-frame swings
Tailor each trail to the weapon's character

principles.principle: Sweep a fading polygon ribbon behind every sword swing
principles.why: Blade trails are vital; attacks won't have the same oomph without them.
principles.how: Draw polygons behind the blade like a folding fan with the sword as the leading edge, and make the tail translucent so it fades; add similar blur to punches and kicks.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving swings with no trail at all.
principles.example: Smash Bros. adds blade trails to swords and a similar effect to punches and kicks.
principles.quote: Attacks won't have the same oomph without them, so getting them right can have a tremendous impact.

principles.principle: Adjust swing animations until the trail reads from the camera
principles.why: A fast blade's raw path looks angular, and trails can be almost imperceptible when viewed from the side.
principles.how: Check swings from the gameplay camera and correct the animation so the arc stands out; avoid plain horizontal slashes.
principles.anti_pattern: A plain horizontal slash whose trail vanishes from the side.

principles.principle: Use a single flat trail image for one-frame swings
principles.why: When a swing finishes in a single frame the trail only shows for an instant, but hitstop on a hit lets the eye still register it.
principles.how: For very fast swings, show one 2D mesh image of the trail instead of building a polygon path.

principles.principle: Design each blade trail to express its weapon
principles.why: Sword swings may look similar, but the trail can show what makes each weapon and fighter different.
principles.how: Emphasize the edge for a tip-strong sword, use a frenzied look for a heavy blade, match a two-tone weapon's colors, add flames to a burning sword, and skip the fade for a light-emitting blade.
principles.anti_pattern: One generic trail for every sword.
principles.example: Marth's edge emphasis, Ike's frenzied trail, Pyra's flames, Travis's non-fading beam katana.

summary: Whenever the player isn't in control, let them skip what you're showing (all at once if possible) and let them pause cutscenes, even if you'd love them to watch every second.
takeaways: Make logos, movies, intermissions and cutscenes skippable
Skip all at once if you can
No save data doesn't mean a first viewing
Allow line-by-line skipping of dialogue
Cutscenes must be pausable, not just skippable

principles.principle: Make every non-interactive sequence skippable, all at once
principles.why: Not being able to skip video content is flat-out inconvenient, and a player without save data may still have seen it before.
principles.how: Allow a single press to skip company logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes, even on a fresh save; let in-engine dialogue advance line by line.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing players to watch because you want them to see everything you made.
principles.quote: When the player's not in control, make sure they can skip what you're showing them—I can't emphasize that enough.

principles.principle: Let players pause during cutscenes
principles.why: Phone calls, visitors or dinner can pull players away at any moment, and skip-only cutscenes aren't modern design.
principles.how: Support pausing mid-cutscene everywhere except in online games that keep advancing.
principles.anti_pattern: Cutscenes that can be skipped but not paused.

principles.principle: Write logo guidelines that assume logos are skippable
principles.why: Unskippable logos imposed by company guidelines or regulations aren't popular nowadays.
principles.how: If you set company or platform logo rules, make skippability the default.

summary: In side-view games, mirror characters' animations when they turn around so they always face the camera and show their faces, and plan ahead for the extra work and handedness problems this brings.
takeaways: Mirror animations so both sides face the viewer
Facing away hides expression and information
Mirroring swaps handedness and held items
Unsuitable for asymmetric characters like sword fighters
Angle side-view poses so faces stay visible

principles.principle: Mirror animations so characters face the camera from both sides
principles.why: Without mirroring, the character on the right faces away, so you can't see their expression and get little information.
principles.how: Use mirrored poses and movements when a character changes facing in a side view instead of turning the model around.
principles.anti_pattern: Expressive characters showing their backs on one side of the screen.
principles.example: Smash Bros. adopted flipped animation after Brawl; Street Fighter IV kept Street Fighter II's sprite mirroring.
principles.quote: We can't see his expression, and receive little information. For someone this expressive, he should really be facing us, right?

principles.principle: Budget for the handedness problems mirroring creates
principles.why: Mirroring takes a lot of work: right-handed punches become left-handed and held items must switch hands.
principles.how: Plan quick hand swaps for items and accept flipped handedness; skip mirroring for characters without horizontal symmetry, such as sword fighters.
principles.anti_pattern: Mirroring asymmetric sword fighters.

principles.principle: Angle side-view poses toward the camera to show the face
principles.why: Pure profile views aren't fun to look at and hide the face for half of the movement.
principles.how: Turn runs and similar moves diagonally toward the viewer so the face and visual information stay visible from the side camera.
principles.anti_pattern: Animating runs directly from the side.
principles.example: Kirby's run in Smash Bros. faces diagonally so his face shows from the side view.

principles.principle: Design mirrored graphics so they still read when flipped
principles.why: Text and symbols on mirrored characters or items will be seen reversed.
principles.how: Use horizontally symmetric letters or shapes for logos and emblems that will be mirrored.
principles.example: Dee Jay's MAXIMUM pants in Super Street Fighter II; Kirby's Maxim Tomato built from two mirror images, hence the M.

summary: When customization is part of the fun, make the work of customizing fun as well: show each option's effect, make the trade-offs clear, make choosing fast, let players test right away and make every part look cool.
takeaways: The customization work itself must be fun
Show effects visually, not just as numbers
Offer markedly distinct options with clear pros and cons
Sort items, distinct icons, auto-equip strongest gear
Let players test changes immediately, on the fly

principles.principle: Show customization effects visually instead of with numbers alone
principles.why: Customization feels like a chore unless players can see what their work will result in, and numbers alone are less intuitive.
principles.how: Draw the attack range or other effect directly on the customization screen when a part is selected.
principles.anti_pattern: Showing attack power differences only as numbers.
principles.quote: In games like these, the work players put into customization is a big part of the appeal— so it's imperative that the work itself is fun.

principles.principle: Give every option clear pros and cons that make it distinct
principles.why: Options with meaningful, markedly distinct differences set a game's customization apart.
principles.how: Design trade-offs such as wide spread with short range versus narrow spread with long range, and state both sides.
principles.anti_pattern: Options that differ in name only.
principles.example: Wide-spread short-range weapon vs. narrow long-range weapon.

principles.principle: Make picking parts fast with sorting, distinct icons and auto-equip
principles.why: Lots of items is good for collectibles, but players accumulate so much that selection becomes slow and similar icons cause struggle.
principles.how: Add sorting and categories, keep every icon visually distinct, and include an automatic equip-strongest option.
principles.anti_pattern: Look-alike icons and unsorted inventories.

principles.principle: Let players test customizations immediately and make parts look cool
principles.why: Quick testing makes changes meaningful, and nobody wants to use something that doesn't look good.
principles.how: Allow trying a build right away, ideally swapping parts on the fly, and give every part a cool or cute design, including cosmetic-only options.

summary: Early-1980s pixel art was typed in as hexadecimal numbers, one bit per pixel, with stacked bit layers for color and simple compression, and knowing those roots shows how much complexity modern graphics have added.
takeaways: Early microcomputer pixel art was entered as hex numbers
One hex digit encodes a 4x1 pixel strip
Two stacked bit layers give three colors plus transparency
Run compression: 0x8 instead of 00000000
Easy input today, but far more complex graphics

principles.principle: Stack two 1-bit layers for three colors plus transparency
principles.why: Overlaying two same-sized pixel layers gives four combinations per pixel: both empty, first filled, second filled, or both filled.
principles.how: In tight-memory or retro formats, store each sprite as two bitplanes and map the four combinations to transparent plus three colors.
principles.example: NES-style three-color sprites.

principles.principle: Compress repeated runs instead of storing every pixel value
principles.why: Writing a run as a value and a count is much shorter than writing every value out.
principles.how: Encode runs of identical data as value-times-count, such as 0x8 instead of 00000000.

principles.principle: Plan pixel art on a grid before converting it to data
principles.why: Without graphics tools, drawing on graph paper first and counting out values afterward was the common way to get correct data.
principles.how: Lay out the image on a grid first, then derive the values row by row.
principles.example: Sakurai used a cross as a guide and estimated values on a borrowed pocket computer.
principles.quote: Everyone used data—numbers, that is— to enter the value of each pixel.

summary: Different monitors and room lighting change how color looks, so give your team a process for matching colors: a shared reference screen, calibration by eye and neutral lighting, so art isn't judged on screens that are lying.
takeaways: Even identical monitors vary in color and brightness
Color variance is critical for artists and supervisors
Calibrate by sight against a shared, visible monitor
Some monitor gaps can't be calibrated away
Use neutral lighting; tinted rooms skew the art

principles.principle: Calibrate team monitors by eye against one shared reference screen
principles.why: Every monitor shows color slightly differently, and measuring devices are of limited use because games are often output on ordinary TVs.
principles.how: Place one monitor far enough away for everyone to see and calibrate color by sight against it; stop using monitors whose gaps can't be fixed.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming everyone sees the same colors.
principles.example: A Mewtwo image lost its right-side shadow and contrast on one monitor, which no calibration fixed.
principles.quote: But within the dev team, at least, it's good to have a process of eliminating color disparity as much as possible.

principles.principle: Light art workspaces as neutrally as possible
principles.why: Ambient lighting changes how color is perceived, so artists compensate and their work drifts off.
principles.how: Replace tinted or moody lights in areas where art is made or reviewed with neutral lighting.
principles.anti_pattern: Moody yellow office lights.
principles.example: A company lit with yellow lights produced art with a bluish tint.
principles.quote: When it comes to lighting, I suggest you choose something as neutral as possible.

summary: Sound is hard to describe, so give sound designers concrete descriptions of a sound's role, comparisons everyone knows and links to real examples, then approve whatever fits the game even if it isn't what you first imagined.
takeaways: Audio feedback is hard; it has no physical form
Use concrete phrases and widely known comparisons
Attach links to real sound examples
Onomatopoeia alone fails in text, but adds clues
Approve sounds that fit the game, not your image

principles.principle: Request sounds with concrete roles, known comparisons and example links
principles.why: Audio has no physical form and can't be approximated by voice, and not everyone knows every specific real sound.
principles.how: Describe the role ('strong attack'), compare only to universally known sounds ('like a jet engine'), and attach a link such as a YouTube clip of a similar sound.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming the team knows the specific sound you mean.

principles.principle: Don't rely on onomatopoeia alone in written sound feedback
principles.why: With remote work, asking for more 'clang' or 'boom' shows you had something in mind but doesn't convey it; still, onomatopoeia can sometimes bridge sound and emotion.
principles.how: Use onomatopoeia only as an extra clue next to a concrete description, since the team wants as many details as possible.
principles.anti_pattern: Emails that just ask for more clang or boom.
principles.example: Sakurai's sound lead said onomatopoeia can be helpful every now and then.
principles.quote: There's little point in writing an email asking for more clang or boom.

principles.principle: Approve sounds that fit the game even if they differ from your idea
principles.why: Sounds directly convey feedback and feeling, so fit matters most, and sometimes the result is better than what was imagined.
principles.how: Judge each delivered sound by whether it suits the game, while starting every request with a clear idea of the target.
principles.anti_pattern: Rejecting sounds only because they don't match the one in your head.

summary: Every game you sell needs a trailer, and that trailer should get to real gameplay as fast as possible, not spend its opening on logos, cinematics and story.
takeaways: A gameplay trailer is absolutely essential for selling
Get to actual gameplay as soon as possible
New IP and indie titles can't rely on teasers
Story and world can come later
Presentations are all about speed

principles.principle: Always ship a trailer that shows the actual game
principles.why: Nearly every game has a promotional video, and Sakurai won't buy a game without one unless there's a very good reason.
principles.how: Treat a gameplay trailer as a required deliverable, including on your store page.
principles.anti_pattern: Store-page trailers with no gameplay footage at all.
principles.example: Some Steam page trailers show no gameplay.

principles.principle: Show gameplay as soon as possible in every trailer
principles.why: Long logos and intros make viewers skip ahead, and trailers exist to show what the game is about; a trailer will never be on the level of a film.
principles.how: Cut opening logos, movies and character intros, lead with what makes the game appealing, and leave story and world for later.
principles.anti_pattern: Opening movies and character intros that take forever to reach gameplay.
principles.quote: And please, get to the actual game as soon as possible!

principles.principle: Rely on teasers only if your name already sells
principles.why: Popular series and famous creators can get by with teasers, but new IP, especially indie titles, must show gameplay to be understood.
principles.how: For a new or indie title, open with gameplay, footage that illustrates the systems, or an honest tech demo of how the game really runs.
principles.anti_pattern: Teaser-only reveals for a new IP.

summary: Fix a clear concept before production starts and steer by it like a lighthouse for the whole project. Bring out emergent fun along the way, but don't change direction midway, or you'll waste your team's work and get lost.
takeaways: The concept gives a game its appeal and direction
Never change direction midway through development
Bring out emergent fun, but stay on course
Scrapping work wastes months and demotivates the team
Design docs can't fully convey a game's fun

principles.principle: Never change your concept's direction midway through development
principles.why: The concept is like a lighthouse; changing your trajectory gets you lost, and things only get worse from there.
principles.how: When fatigue or doubt sets in, check decisions against the original concept instead of switching direction.
principles.anti_pattern: Changing direction because the game isn't turning out as expected.
principles.example: Concepts like the fun of sending opponents flying or the thrill of sprinting down a straight path.
principles.quote: Come storm or dark of night, the one thing you should never change is your trajectory toward that light.

principles.principle: Don't start production until the concept is clearly in sight
principles.why: Restarting means discarding things artists and programmers spent months on, which is costly and demotivates the team.
principles.how: Make sure the director can state the game's appeal clearly before committing the team; amplify emergent fun rather than restarting.
principles.anti_pattern: Moving forward without a clear concept, then scrapping work.

principles.principle: As director, keep the team oriented on the concept
principles.why: Team members often can't grasp a new game's appeal from design docs until it exists, and unplanned elements can become core fun.
principles.how: Repeatedly restate the concept and steer the team back toward it so their work stays usable.
principles.anti_pattern: Expecting the design document alone to convey the fun.
principles.example: People told Sakurai after release, 'Now I see what you were getting at.'

summary: In a licensed game, faithfulness to the source and satisfying fans' love for it come first and fun comes second, so look for source settings that naturally become gameplay and use the gaps the source leaves to invent.
takeaways: Source material restricts licensed game design
Fans want faithfulness first, fun second
It's product value versus fun
Some settings map perfectly to gameplay
Freedom comes where the source shows little

principles.principle: Put faithfulness to the source first in licensed games
principles.why: Fans see the game as one form of a property among comics, anime, figures and events, and want faithfulness and their love satisfied more than great push and pull.
principles.how: Set faithfulness as the top goal, then make the gameplay as fun as possible within it, and time the release alongside the property's other media.
principles.anti_pattern: Freely changing the original's story and characters.
principles.quote: It's product value versus fun. It's great if you can achieve both, but you'll never get a perfect score on all fronts.

principles.principle: Build on source settings that naturally map to gameplay
principles.why: Sometimes the original setting forms the basis for a very fun game, though it still takes developer skill to add game-only ideas.
principles.how: Find a concept in the source that works as a mechanic, then layer on systems unique to the game.
principles.example: Megami Tensei's novel concept of summoning demons from a computer, plus the game-only idea of demon fusion.

principles.principle: Invent freely where the source shows little
principles.why: Licensed characters can't be changed much, but those with little shown action leave room to design.
principles.how: Identify characters or elements the source barely defines and create their moves there.
principles.example: In Super Smash Bros., pilots Fox and Captain Falcon gave freedom, producing the Falcon Punch.

summary: Use randomness to keep repeated play fresh and make players adapt, but never let luck alone decide a loss, keep it out of strict skill contests, and seed it so players can't manipulate it.
takeaways: Randomness keeps repeated play fresh
It adds strategy by forcing adaptation
Players must feel responsible for their own failure
Keep randomness out of strict skill competitions
Seed randomness with the clock to prevent manipulation

principles.principle: Use randomness to keep repeated play fresh and strategic
principles.why: Games repeat the same content, and static rules struggle to deliver variety; randomness makes each play different and challenges players to handle a range of situations.
principles.how: Vary probabilities instead of fixing results in places where repetition goes stale.

principles.principle: Never let luck alone decide a player's loss
principles.why: Losing only because of bad luck is hard to accept; players need to feel responsible for their own failure.
principles.how: Give players ways to respond to random events or control them, and keep randomness out of strict skill contests.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on a luck stat players forget or won't invest in.
principles.example: Peach's Smash Attack, once random, is now chosen with up or down; Wizardry's 1981 luck stat.
principles.quote: In a game, players need to feel to some extent like they're responsible for their own failure.

principles.principle: Keep randomness that still demands skill or enables comebacks
principles.why: Random elements are acceptable when using them well takes skill, and random items give anyone a chance to come back in a fun-first game.
principles.how: Allow randomness like a random command list that each needs skill, and random items in casual modes.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: the Hero's randomized command list and markedly random items.

principles.principle: Seed random values with an indefinite input like the clock
principles.why: Computers can't produce true randomness, so players can reset or perform actions to always get the result they want.
principles.how: Factor the system's internal clock or similar indefinite value into random number generation.
principles.anti_pattern: Predictable random results that resetting can exploit.

summary: When you have things to give your team, turn the giveaway into a small game: it works as an icebreaker and builds the kind of director–team relationship game development should have.
takeaways: Give spare games and hardware to the team
Run giveaways as a sign-up lottery
Decide winners with games, sometimes with secret rules
Fun giveaways act as team icebreakers
Good director–team relationships are how dev should be

principles.principle: Turn team giveaways into quick games instead of random handouts
principles.why: Making games and events out of giveaways serves as an icebreaker, and everyone who has fun wins.
principles.how: List items on a shared daily page, let interested people sign up, then pick winners by rock-paper-scissors, a match in your game, a tricky-move race or a secret rule.
principles.anti_pattern: Handing items out at random.
principles.example: Sakurai used the Daily Report page, Smash Bros. battles, Samurai Kirby and a secret closest-to-0-seconds rule.
principles.quote: After all, if you're giving something away, the real winner is anyone who has fun.

principles.principle: Invest in a warm relationship between director and team
principles.why: A good director–team relationship is how game development should be, and it shows in things like the team giving the director birthday presents.
principles.how: Share spare items and run small fun events with the team regularly.
principles.example: Sakurai's team gave him a wide variety of birthday presents.

summary: Make decisions on the spot instead of saying "later", because every minute of waiting leaves the team blocked, but stay flexible enough to correct a call once you see it was wrong.
takeaways: Don't end meetings with 'I'll decide later'
Push whoever has authority to decide now
Every minute of waiting leaves issues unresolved
Give deciders accurate, reliable information
Stay flexible; correct mistakes with slight adjustments

principles.principle: Make decisions on the spot, not later
principles.why: Each decision sends the team down a long production path, and every minute they wait is a minute the issue stays unresolved; a quick, firm call helps more people than you'd imagine.
principles.how: Push whoever has authority in the meeting to decide before it ends; if you're the decider, decide as soon as a team member comes to you and research immediately if needed.
principles.anti_pattern: Saying 'I'll have to decide on this later!'
principles.quote: When it comes to making decisions, it's best to think that "later" is too late!

principles.principle: Feed decision-makers accurate, reliable information
principles.why: If the relevant resources aren't reliable, the decision itself won't be either.
principles.how: When raising an issue for a decision, bring verified information so the call can be made quickly and soundly.

principles.principle: Correct wrong decisions with frequent slight adjustments
principles.why: Decisions set the project's trajectory, so small course corrections keep it on the right path.
principles.how: When you notice a mistake, revise the decision instead of sticking to it because it was already made.
principles.anti_pattern: Staying the course on a known error.

summary: Use blur to show motion and fill the gaps between frames, through drawn blur textures or hardware effects, but keep it subtle and natural (or let players adjust it), because too much blur makes the action hard to read.
takeaways: Blur shows afterimages and fills gaps between frames
Swap in blurred textures for spinning objects
Blur can be hand-drawn or hardware-calculated
Don't overdo it; fuzzy visuals hide the action
Offer a blur-strength option

principles.principle: Swap in blurred textures on fast-moving or spinning parts
principles.why: Blur shows the afterimage of motion and fills the gaps between frames, making animation feel less stop-and-start.
principles.how: Replace the texture with a blurred version while an object spins, or build blur into textures of parts that are always moving.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving spinning parts unblurred.
principles.example: Sakurai wishes Kirby Air Ride's Wheel star had spinning blur; Smash Ultimate's Spirit Train wheels and rails have blur built in.

principles.principle: Keep artificial blur subtle and let players adjust it
principles.why: Overdone blur can make things look worse and make it hard to know what's going on, and teams struggle to agree on what looks good.
principles.how: Dial blur back wherever it obscures play, and add a blur-strength setting in the options menu.
principles.anti_pattern: Fuzzy visuals from heavy artificial blur.
principles.quote: The more natural a blur effect, the more believable it'll be, and the less discomfort players will feel.

summary: Every action-game verb (jumping, dashing, melee, shooting, dodging, parrying, hiding) should pair a danger with an opportunity, so understand why each one's risk and reward works instead of just copying it.
takeaways: Game essence is taking risks and earning rewards
Every action pairs danger with opportunity
Parrying turns massive risk into massive reward
Longer range weapons often come with less ammo
Understand the meaning; go beyond mere imitation

principles.principle: Give every core action both a danger and an opportunity
principles.why: Game essence is taking risks and earning rewards, and in each action danger and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.
principles.how: Pair benefits with costs: edge jumps clear more but risk falling, dashing is faster but harder to control or costs stamina, melee requires closing in.
principles.anti_pattern: Actions whose benefit has no matching risk.

principles.principle: Pay for range and safety with resources or exposure
principles.why: Unilateral attacks from afar would remove risk, so they need a cost.
principles.how: Give longer-range weapons less ammo, let enemies shoot back, and make hiding limit your ability to attack.

principles.principle: Reward last-moment defensive timing heavily
principles.why: Dodges and parries that work right before an attack lands let players turn massive risk into massive reward.
principles.how: Make parries trigger only at the moment of impact with a big payoff, and give dodges a brief window where other actions are harder.
principles.quote: By waiting until right when an attack is going to hit you, you can experience the fun of turning massive risk into massive reward.

principles.principle: Understand why a borrowed mechanic works before copying it
principles.why: Considering the meaning behind each kind of game essence increases your chances of making something even more fun.
principles.how: For each mechanic you borrow, write down its risk and reward and design your version from that reasoning.
principles.anti_pattern: Mere imitation.
principles.quote: Try to go beyond mere imitation!

summary: Blend between animations so transitions such as cancels look natural from any starting pose, but keep blends short and snappy, because long automatic blends kill rhythm and impact and can distort the motion.
takeaways: Blending combines two or more animations
Cancels blend into the next action, not snap
Too-smooth blends lose rhythm and impact
Keep blends quick and snappy
Blending shines most in fully 3D games

principles.principle: Blend into the next animation on cancels instead of snapping
principles.why: Blending lets the same follow-up animation start naturally from drastically different poses.
principles.how: When an input arrives during cancel frames, blend from the current pose of the canceled action into the new animation.
principles.anti_pattern: Hard snaps from one animation to the next.
principles.example: In Smash Bros., idle-to-walk and attack-to-walk both look natural despite very different starting poses.

principles.principle: Keep blends short so animation keeps its rhythm and impact
principles.why: Making animation too smooth decreases rhythm and impact, and automated blending can distort the motion.
principles.how: Set short blend durations and appropriate strength, and check blends for distorted poses.
principles.anti_pattern: Long, overly smooth blends.
principles.quote: As a result, you don't want a blend to last too long. Make it quick and snappy.

principles.principle: Use positional blending for directional and terrain-aware motion
principles.why: Directional inputs and 3D terrain create too many pose combinations to animate by hand.
principles.how: Blend a center stance with poses around a circle for directional moves, and in 3D, blend upper and lower body separately and adapt legs and turns to terrain.
principles.example: Smash Bros. shield shifting blends circular movement with the fixed center stance.

summary: Give your team a well-organized debug mode, built into the normal controller through button combinations, because it's used every day and has a huge effect on productivity even though it's stripped from the final game.
takeaways: Debug mode tests and analyzes the game during development
Missing debug features force time-wasting workarounds
Some debug tools can become player features
Put debug controls on the gameplay controller
Keep debug modes organized and pruned

principles.principle: Build debug commands for your most common test setups
principles.why: Without certain debug features you have to spend time coming up with other solutions.
principles.how: Add direct commands for frequent setups, like setting every fighter to a given damage percentage.
principles.anti_pattern: Workarounds such as temporarily changing a move's damage to set up tests.
principles.example: Before Smash had a damage-setting feature, the team set Fox's forward tilt to deal 100% damage.

principles.principle: Map debug functions onto the normal gameplay controller
principles.why: Hunting down a separate debug controller whenever you need it is a real pain.
principles.how: Assign debug functions to button combinations on the same controller used for play.
principles.anti_pattern: A dedicated second controller for debug mode.

principles.principle: Keep the debug mode organized, pruned and out of the final build
principles.why: Teams use debug mode every day, so its convenience has a huge impact on productivity, but these modes easily bloat.
principles.how: Regularly reorganize and prune debug menus, and strip them before release.
principles.anti_pattern: A bloated, disorganized debug menu.
principles.quote: the convenience a debug mode provides will have a huge impact on a team's productivity.

principles.principle: Promote easy-to-understand debug tools into player features
principles.why: Some debug visualizations help players learn, as long as they're easy to understand.
principles.how: Review debug overlays for ones that could ship in a training mode, weighing whether they reveal too much.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Training Mode's trajectory guide began as a debug feature Sakurai requested.

summary: It's fine to start by imitating a game you admire, but by the end of development your game needs many kinds of appeal the original lacks, or players will just play the original.
takeaways: Making similar games refined the industry; it's good
Any finished game beats no game
Players may just stick with the original
An homage needs many appeals the original lacks
Make something players can't get anywhere else

principles.principle: Give an homage many kinds of appeal the original lacks
principles.why: The original is compelling, which is why you referenced it, so players may decide to stick with it unless yours offers more.
principles.how: List the reasons a player would choose your game over the original and work to add many, not just one.
principles.anti_pattern: Riding on the original's coattails.

principles.principle: Compensate elsewhere when you borrow the original's systems
principles.why: Designing the systems is the most difficult part of making games, so skipping it leaves a gap you must make up for.
principles.how: Invest the effort saved on systems into unique appeal across other dimensions.

principles.principle: Start by imitating, but finish with something unique
principles.why: Appeal is multi-faceted and can't be measured on one scale; it's not about surpassing the original.
principles.how: Use imitation as your starting point, and near the end of development check that your game offers what players can't get elsewhere.
principles.quote: But by the end of development, you should strive to make something that players can't get anywhere else.

summary: Every game, however simple, should let players reassign buttons, ideally through a graphical controller screen, cursor-based assignment, shared actions and saveable profiles.
takeaways: Every game should have a key config
Show controllers graphically, not as vertical lists
Assign with cursor, not press-to-assign
Let multiple buttons share one action
Save layouts to profiles, even on the controller

principles.principle: Ship a key config in every game, however simple
principles.why: Button settings are a necessity for some players, and consoles don't yet offer per-game remapping; console-wide remaps affect every game and can leave actions unmapped.
principles.how: Build an in-game button settings screen and make sure no action can end up without a button.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving remapping to a console-wide setting.
principles.example: Switch's console-wide remap applies to all applications.
principles.quote: However, it's a necessity for some of our players. Whenever possible, I urge you to add support for this feature.

principles.principle: Show the controller graphically and assign buttons with a cursor
principles.why: Vertical lists make it hard to track which button does what, and press-to-assign screens can capture the menu's own exit button.
principles.how: Draw the controller, let players select a button with the cursor, then choose its action from a list.
principles.anti_pattern: A vertical list with press-the-button assignment.
principles.example: Smash Bros. depicts all controllers graphically.

principles.principle: Allow shared actions and portable control profiles
principles.why: Smash Bros. is played together, so guest players need a fast way to load their controls.
principles.how: Let multiple buttons map to one action, save layouts under profile names selectable before a fight, and store them on the controller when possible.
principles.example: Smash Bros. has two jump buttons and name-based control profiles.
